stem: A liver waitlist candidate is placed on inactive status while temporarily unsuitable for transplant. According to OPTN Policy 3.6.A, how does waiting time accrue during inactivity?

options.text: No waiting time accrues while the candidate remains inactive
Unlimited waiting time accrues, as for kidney candidates
Waiting time accrues only for the first 30 cumulative inactive days
Waiting time doubles each month the candidate remains inactive

explanation.rationale_correct: OPTN Table 3-3 specifies that liver candidates accrue no waiting time while inactive, similar to heart candidates and unlike kidney or lung candidates who accrue unlimited inactive waiting time.

rationale_incorrect.B: Unlimited inactive accrual applies to kidney and lung candidates, not liver candidates.
rationale_incorrect.C: A 30-day cumulative inactive accrual limit applies to intestine candidates, not liver candidates.
rationale_incorrect.D: Liver inactive waiting time does not double monthly; it does not accrue at all.

primary_anchor.section: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3 Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates → Liver
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Liver … No time … Candidates accrue waiting time while inactive

references.locator: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3: Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates (liver candidates accrue no waiting time while inactive); PDF p. 47 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

stem: An intestine waitlist candidate is placed on inactive status while temporarily unsuitable for transplant. According to OPTN Policy 3.6.A, how does waiting time accrue during inactivity?

options.text: Up to 30 cumulative days of waiting time while inactive
No waiting time accrues while the candidate remains inactive
Unlimited waiting time accrues, as for kidney candidates
Waiting time accrues only when the candidate is younger than 18 years

explanation.rationale_correct: OPTN Table 3-3 specifies that intestine candidates accrue up to 30 cumulative days of waiting time while inactive, unlike kidney and lung candidates who accrue unlimited inactive waiting time.

rationale_incorrect.B: No inactive accrual applies to heart and liver candidates, not intestine candidates.
rationale_incorrect.C: Unlimited inactive accrual applies to kidney and lung candidates; intestine accrual is capped at 30 cumulative days.
rationale_incorrect.D: Intestine inactive waiting-time rules apply regardless of candidate age.

primary_anchor.section: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3 Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates → Intestine
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Intestine … Up to 30 cumulative days … Candidates accrue waiting time while inactive

references.locator: Policy 3.6.A → Table 3-3: Waiting Time for Inactive Candidates (intestine candidates accrue up to 30 cumulative inactive days); PDF p. 47 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. First intestine OPTN waitlist item; intestine inactive 30-day rule distinct from lung unlimited (cctc-2071) and liver no-accrual (cctc-2073); anchor verified on optn-policies p. 47.

stem: When coordinating post-transplant monitoring for a kidney recipient, which BK virus management principle aligns with standard references?

options.text: Routine screening for BK virus replication to guide immunosuppression reduction
BK virus screening is unnecessary because effective antiviral therapy exists
BK replication requires immediate graft nephrectomy in every case
Immunosuppression should be intensified whenever BK replication is detected

explanation.rationale_correct: No effective antiviral therapies exist for BK virus, so routine screening for BK virus replication is imperative to guide reduction of immunosuppression.

rationale_incorrect.B: Lack of effective antiviral therapy makes routine BK screening essential rather than unnecessary.
rationale_incorrect.C: Management emphasizes screening and immunosuppression reduction rather than mandatory nephrectomy in every case.
rationale_incorrect.D: Detected BK replication typically prompts immunosuppression reduction, not intensification.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → J. Polyomaviruses → 2. BK virus → e.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: No effective antiviral therapies … screening for BK virus replication be performed routinely in order to guide reduction of immunosuppression

stem: When presenting deceased-donor information to a candidate, which initial donor risk-assessment step aligns with standard references?

options.text: Immediate graft implantation without any donor data review
Relying solely on recipient preference without donor assessment
Deferring all infection-risk review until one year after transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Donor risk assessment for transmitted infections begins with donor chart review, followed by discussion with available contacts and physical examination by the procurement team.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donor chart review is the foundational first step in donor risk assessment before organ acceptance.
rationale_incorrect.C: Donor infection-risk assessment requires structured review rather than recipient preference alone.
rationale_incorrect.D: Donor-transmitted infection risk is assessed before transplantation, not deferred for one year.
